notes.47:3: The Greek clause "I will no longer hand over to men" is elliptical (implying God's people as the object) and differs from the Hebrew text's "I will not spare any man."
notes.47:6: The Greek reads second-person "you defiled My inheritance," attributing the defilement to Babylon rather than to God as in the Hebrew text ("I profaned").
notes.47:9: The Greek omits the Hebrew clause "both of these in a single day, loss of children and widowhood," leaving bereavement from verse 8 as the implied subject of "it shall come suddenly upon you."
notes.47:14: In place of the Hebrew statement that there is no coal for warming or fire to sit before, the Greek renders an ironic command: "because you have coals of fire, sit upon them!"
notes.48:9: The Septuagint reads "I will show you My wrath, and My glorious deeds I will bring upon you," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "I will defer My anger, and for My praise I will restrain it for you."
notes.48:10: The Septuagint reads "I have sold you, not for the sake of silver; yet I have delivered you out of the furnace of poverty," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tested you in the furnace of affliction").
notes.48:16: Greek kyrios Kyrios (literally "Lord, the Lord") renders the Hebrew divine title Adonai YHWH and is translated here as "the Sovereign Lord" (likewise in 50:5 and 50:7).
notes.48:21: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which recalls past provision in the wilderness, the Septuagint casts the promise in the future tense and concludes with "and My people shall drink."
notes.49:1: The Septuagint renders the second clause "After a long time it shall stand, says the Lord," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "peoples from afar."
notes.49:6: The Septuagint reads "It is a great thing for you" (rather than "too small a thing" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text) and includes "for a covenant of a race" before "for a light of the nations."
notes.49:7: The Septuagint opens the oracle with the imperative "Sanctify him who despises his own life" and places "the servants of rulers" in apposition to "the nations."
notes.49:12: The Septuagint specifies "from the land of the Persians" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "from the land of Sinim."
notes.50:2: The Septuagint asks "Is My hand not strong enough to redeem?" and states that the fish "shall be dried up," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text asks whether God's hand is "too short" and says the fish "stink."
notes.50:4: The Septuagint reads "to know when it is necessary to speak a word," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("to know how to sustain the weary with a word").
notes.50:6: The Septuagint renders "to scourges" and "to blows," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "to those who strike" and "to those who pluck out the beard."
notes.51:1: The Greek uses active verbs ("which you hewed out... which you dug"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses passives referring to Israel being hewn from the rock.
notes.51:6: The Greek reads "was made firm like smoke" (estereothe), a notable Septuagint rendering compared with the Hebrew "will vanish like smoke."
notes.51:9: Unlike the Hebrew text, which addresses the arm of the Lord, the Greek directly addresses Jerusalem here and in verse 10.
notes.51:15: The Greek transliterates the Hebrew title as Sabaoth ("of hosts"), preserved here as "the Lord of Sabaoth" (also in 54:5).
notes.51:20: The Greek vividly compares the fainting sons to "a half-boiled beet" (seutlion hemiephthon), differing markedly from the Hebrew "an antelope in a net."
notes.52:4: The doubled Greek title kyrios Kyrios ("the Lord, the Lord") reflects the compound Hebrew divine title Adonai YHWH.
notes.52:6: The Greek word hora ("season," also "prime" or "beauty") links the divine announcement "I am present" directly to the messenger imagery of verse 7.
notes.52:14: The Greek addresses the Servant in the second person ("You," "Your") and describes His appearance as "without glory from men."
notes.52:15: The Greek reads "marvel" (thaumasontai) rather than the Hebrew "sprinkle," and the second half of the verse is quoted closely in Romans 15:21.
notes.53:1: The Septuagint opens with the vocative 'Lord' (Kyrie), echoed in John 12:38 and Romans 10:16.
notes.53:2: Greek anengeilamen ('we made announcement') is a distinctly Septuagint reading where the Hebrew has 'he grew up.' Messianic pronouns for the Servant are capitalized throughout the chapter.
notes.53:5: Greek paidia here is an orthographic variant of paideia ('chastisement/discipline'); molopi is singular ('bruise' or 'welt').
notes.53:8: This Septuagint wording ('In His humiliation His judgment was taken away') is the form quoted in Acts 8:32-33.
notes.53:10: The Saints Greek Critical Text reads second-person plural dote ('if you give') and first-person plural he psyche hemon ('our soul'), where other editions read 'your soul' and the Hebrew reads 'his soul.'
notes.54:4: The Greek reads "everlasting shame" (aischynen aionion) rather than the Hebrew "shame of your youth."
notes.54:6: The Greek begins with a negation ("The Lord has not called you as a forsaken... woman"), contrasting with the affirmative simile in the Hebrew text.
notes.54:10: The Greek continues the negative oath from verse 9 ("nor shall your hills be shaken") and closes with a well-known Septuagint reading using the vocative Kyrie ("O Lord") rather than the nominative Kyrios ("the Lord").
notes.54:15: The Greek reads "proselytes shall come to you through Me," presenting a promise of Gentile converts seeking refuge in Zion rather than the warning about attackers in the Hebrew.
notes.55:1: Greek στέαρ reads "fat," reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants (chelev, "fat") rather than the Masoretic "milk" (chalav).
notes.55:3: Greek τὰ ὅσια Δαυὶδ τὰ πιστά ("the faithful holy things of David") is the exact Septuagint phrasing later quoted in Acts 13:34.
notes.55:9: Greek uses ἀπέχει ("is distant") rather than "is higher," and sets plural "your thoughts" against singular "My mind."
notes.55:11: Greek omits "empty" and ends with a direct divine promise, "and I will prosper your ways and My commandments."
notes.56:1: Greek reads "My mercy" (τὸ ἔλεός μου) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "My righteousness."
notes.56:6: Greek explicitly specifies both "male servants and female servants" (δούλους καὶ δούλας) where the Masoretic Text has only "servants."
notes.56:10: Greek opens with the imperative ἴδετε ("See") rather than "his watchmen," reflecting an alternative reading of the underlying Hebrew consonants.
notes.56:11: Greek reads πονηροί ("wicked") rather than "shepherds," and the Septuagint chapter ends at verse eleven without the Masoretic verse twelve.
notes.57:2: Greek reads "his burial shall be in peace; he has been taken away from the midst," differing markedly from the Masoretic image of resting upon beds.
notes.57:6: Greek asks "shall I not be angry?" (οὐκ ὀργισθήσομαι;), whereas the Masoretic Text asks whether the Lord should be appeased.
notes.57:15: Greek displays a distinctive sequence of divine epithets, including "Holy among the holy ones is His name" and "gives longsuffering to the fainthearted."
notes.57:21: Greek renders the closing proverb with χαίρειν ("rejoicing") rather than "peace," and reads simply "God" rather than "my God."
notes.58:5: Greek reads "like a ring" (κρίκον) rather than the Hebrew "like a reed" and frames the verse as a declarative statement rather than a question.
notes.58:6: Greek reads "I have not chosen such a fast... rather..." (pointing back to verse 5) and renders the final clause as tearing apart "every unjust written bond" (συγγραφήν) rather than breaking a yoke.
notes.58:11: Greek reads "your God shall be with you continually" and "just as your soul desires," diverging from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "will guide you" and "in scorched places."
notes.58:12: Greek reads "bring your pathways in the midst to rest" (παύσεις, which can also mean "cause to cease"), where the Hebrew has "restorer of streets to dwell in."
notes.59:5: Greek οὔριον literally denotes a "wind-egg" (an unfertilized or rotten egg), and βασιλίσκος ("basilisk") translates the deadly viper of the Hebrew text.
notes.59:16: Greek ἠμύνατο αὐτούς ("He defended them") and τῇ ἐλεημοσύνῃ ("with mercy") reflect the Septuagint's distinctive rendering of "His own arm brought salvation for Him" and "His righteousness."
notes.59:17: Verses 17-18 in the Septuagint condense the longer Hebrew text, omitting the cloak of zeal and the parallel clauses concerning wrath and the coastlands.
notes.59:20: Greek reads "for the sake of Zion" (ἕνεκεν Σειών) and "turn away impieties from Jacob," diverging from the Hebrew "to Zion, to those who turn from transgression in Jacob" (cf. Romans 11:26).
notes.60:1: Greek opens with a doubled imperative and vocative, "Shine, shine, O Jerusalem" (Φωτίζου φωτίζου, Ἰερουσαλήμ), rather than the Hebrew "Arise, shine."
notes.60:7: Greek reads "the house of My prayer" (ὁ οἶκος τῆς προσευχῆς μου), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "the house of My glory."
notes.60:8: Greek reads "with nestlings to Me" (σὺν νοσσοῖς ἐπ᾽ ἐμέ), diverging from the Hebrew "to their windows/roosts."
notes.60:18: Greek renders the name of the gates as "Engraving" (Γλύμμα, carved work), reflecting a distinct Septuagint reading where the Hebrew has "Praise."
notes.60:21: Greek reads "guarding the planting" (φυλάσσων τὸ φύτευμα), taking the Hebrew noun for "shoot/branch" from the verb meaning "to guard."
notes.61:1: The Greek Septuagint reads "recovery of sight to the blind" (quoted in Luke 4:18), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the opening of prison to those who are bound."
notes.61:3: The Greek reads "generations of righteousness" where the Hebrew has "oaks" or "terebinths of righteousness."
notes.61:7: The Greek condenses the opening of the verse and renders the Hebrew "double" as "a second time."
notes.61:11: The doubled Greek title "the Lord, the Lord" (kyrios Kyrios) reflects the Hebrew compound divine name.
notes.62:1: The Greek reads "My salvation," continuing the Lord's first-person speech, whereas the Hebrew reads "her salvation."
notes.62:7: The Greek reads "there is none like you," interpreting the underlying Hebrew term as "likeness" rather than "rest" or "silence."
notes.62:11: The Greek personalizes the noun as "the Savior" rather than the abstract "your salvation" found in the Hebrew.
notes.63:3: The elliptical Greek phrase "full of the trodden winepress" reflects a different reading of the Hebrew "I have trodden the winepress alone."
notes.63:9: The Greek reads "Neither an envoy nor an angel, but He Himself saved them," stressing God's direct deliverance in contrast to the Hebrew "the angel of His presence saved them."
notes.63:18: The Greek reads "that for a little while we may inherit Your holy mountain," lacking the Hebrew clause about adversaries trampling the sanctuary.
notes.63:19: Following Septuagint versification, the closing clause corresponds to the beginning of 64:1 in Hebrew-based Bibles and runs mid-sentence into the following chapter.
notes.64:3: Greek reads "for those who wait for mercy," and the third-person singular verb "It shall meet" in 64:4 naturally continues with "mercy" as its implied subject.
notes.64:8: Greek reads "in due time" (en kairo), reflecting a reading of "at the time" rather than "forever."
notes.64:9: Following the punctuation of the Greek text, "Zion" stands in apposition to "the city of Your sanctuary," and "for a curse" closes the lament over Jerusalem before the temple is described in 64:10.
notes.65:10: Greek reads "in the forest" (en to drymo) rather than the geographic name "Sharon."
notes.65:11: Greek renders the pagan deities (Gad and Meni) as "the demon" (to daimonio) and "Fortune" (te tyche).
notes.65:15: Greek reads "for a satiety" (eis plesmonen, surfeit or fullness) rather than "for an oath" or "curse."
notes.65:22: Greek explicitly reads "the tree of life" (tou xylou tes zoes) rather than simply "a tree."
notes.66:5: Greek uses an imperative ("Say, O our brethren") addressed to the faithful rather than a report of what hostile brethren said.
notes.66:9: Greek reads "Yet I gave this expectation, and you did not remember Me," differing notably from the rhetorical question in the Hebrew text.
notes.66:18: The opening clause is elliptical in Greek ("And I—their works and their reasoning"), leaving a verb such as "know" unexpressed before "I am coming."
notes.66:19: Greek lists "Put" (Phoud) instead of "Pul," reads "Meshech" (Mosoch) where the Hebrew has "who draw the bow," and renders "Javan" as "Greece" (ten Hellada).
